en: Preface to the Re-engraved Essential Teachings on the Pure Land Now, suffering and joy intersect in all directions; the single spiritual essence undergoes ten thousand transformations. Beings ascend and descend, returning again and again, wearying through the flux of transmigration.
Yet worldly people know only that for a time they possess this human body, never casting their gaze beyond it to observe the greater reality. Thus, amidst the complexities of daily life...

One gives rise to attachment; the objective realm is strong while the mind is weak, and the superior vital energy occasionally declines. The six realms of existence are vast and boundless, and it is uncertain where one’s rebirth will be entrusted.
Nevertheless, the ocean moon and celestial stars remain as the luminous radiance of the mind, and the stations and activities of the six ordinary beings and four sages are empty and spiritual.
If one can take the Buddha’s mind as one’s own mind, then the mind will be strong and the objective realm weak; with the mind swallowing the realm, mindfulness—
Meditate on this with a melting heart. With one Buddha before you, all demons will retreat; there shall be no obstacles in life, and at the end of your life, you will be reborn in the Pure Land.

To simply and diligently recite the name of Amitābha is truly what may be called a miraculous elixir for transforming one's bones. Alas! While millions of paths are easy to find, a single effective method is difficult to seek.

Whether among the Daoists, Confucian scholars, Chan practitioners, teachers of the Dharma, or those of the Vinaya school—the paths of cultivation are vast and wide. Yet, if one abandons the recitation of the Buddha’s name...
Regarding this single Dharma, from where shall its head emerge? Now, I have re-engraved and published the work *The Essentials of the Pure Land*;
herein I briefly discuss its spiritual capacity to inform my kinsmen of the three lives.
Preface by the student of Pure Land, Wuxiang, on the Buddha’s Birthday in the fourth month of the Xinyou year of the Xianfeng reign.
Master Lianchi said: "Distracted thoughts are the disease; mindfulness of the Buddha is the medicine. Mindfulness of the Buddha is precisely the remedy for distracted thoughts.
That one cannot cure them is due to the mindfulness not being intimate. How profound these words are! My elder brother Gengtang has long possessed...

Regarding the faculty of wisdom: he studied the scriptures and daily recited the Buddha’s name with constant and uninterrupted devotion. Recently, he obtained a brief treatise titled *The Essential Points for Encouraging Cultivation of the Pure Land*.

This work teaches that the method for others to practice mindfulness of the Buddha lies in sincerity, faith, and single-mindedness, taking the severance of delusive thoughts as the primary discipline to increase pure causes until reaching the other shore. It is truly a treasure for the cultivation of the mind.

This is a raft. Because it is weighty, I entrust it to the carving block so that you, who share this same aspiration, may ferry yourselves across and ferry others across, transforming and guiding one another in succession until no further demonic activities remain.
Is this not indeed the work of immeasurable merit?
Preface to the *Essential Exhortation to Practice the Pure Land*, written in the seventh month of autumn in the Yimao year of the Xianfeng era (1855). By Pan Zengying.

Exhorting practitioners to cultivate from the fundamental source, and exhorting those who revere the Way.

An Essential Exhortation for the Cultivation of Pure Land:
Compiled by the Pure Land Practitioner Zhenyi Yuan. Question:
Is there such a thing as a person who moves house and forgets his wife? Answer: Yes, there is. Confucius said: "Furthermore..."
There is something even more extreme than this. Jie and Zhou forgot their very persons. If one observes with the eye of the Way, people today have all forgotten their persons.
Why is this? From opening one's eyes in the morning and leaving bed until closing one's eyes at night to go to sleep, there is nothing but worldly toil;
one has never for a moment examined one’s own person. This is what it means to forget one's person. Furthermore, regarding the person and the body, throughout the day—

To speak of it: nothing is greater than hunger and thirst, yet one must prepare for food and drink. Regarding the year, nothing is greater than cold and heat, yet one must prepare for furs and hemp garments.
Regarding one’s entire life, nothing is greater than birth and death, yet one makes no preparation for them—how extreme is such folly!
It is not true folly; it is simply that one does not know there is the cultivation of the Pure Land.
The Dharma serves as a preparation for birth and death. It is like a person traveling to a distant land who must first seek out a place to stay before setting out on their business;
thus, when evening falls and it grows dark, they have a place to lodge. This is what it means to seek a place to stay beforehand.
This refers to the cultivation of the Pure Land. "Arriving at dusk when it is dark" refers to the point when one's great life is about to end.
"Having a place to lodge for the night" refers to being born within a lotus flower, not falling into the miserable realms to undergo various sufferings.

Viewed from this perspective, one recites the Buddha’s name to cultivate the Pure Land, and by cultivating the Pure Land, one attains rebirth there. As the Sūtra says regarding longevity: [text continues].
Life is immeasurable; there is joy and no suffering. To prepare for one’s entire life in this way—is it not truly great? Yet even now, there are those who understand this yet do not practice it.

What is the reason for this? Alas! I have understood it. It may be because they lack a quiet room at home, or because they cannot observe the vegetarian diet, or because their affairs are many and their minds are weary;
thus, they fail to realize that the essential purpose of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) is precisely this.
Practice in a bustling environment. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, if you can remain single-minded and undisturbed amidst noisy places, then one sound is superior to many sounds;
this is what is meant by "when the mind is pure, the land is pure. For example, if one recites the Buddha’s name, one must maintain a strict fast.

This is indeed most excellent. However, this can only be achieved through renunciation. If one remains a householder yet harbors the aspiration for transcendence, one will inevitably be held to an impossible standard of perfection;
such hardship is what people find difficult to endure, and it is not a means to encourage others.

If one can simply rise at dawn and recite the Buddha’s name with sincere devotion, then in this life one may extinguish sins and erase transgressions, and at the end of life, one shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

Regarding the frequency of reciting the Buddha’s name: those who enjoy leisure certainly find that the more they do, the better. However, if one is preoccupied with worldly affairs yet still resolves to attain the supreme Bodhicitta, this must likewise follow the same principle.
To insist on such practice from those who are unable to do so is neither feasible nor a means for encouraging the world.
For even if one is busy all day long, how could there not be a moment’s respite? Why not set aside the time it takes to brew a single cup of tea?

Recently, I have observed that when one recites the Buddha’s name with a mind that does not wander outward, those who labor their minds may rely upon it to nourish them, and those who labor their bodies may likewise rely upon it to conserve their strength.
As a practice that is beneficial and without harm, what could surpass this? Moreover, it is not only that its efficacy is verified at the end of life;
its merit can also be seen in the present world. As the Sūtra says: "If a person receives and upholds my..."
Regarding the name of the Buddha: one shall obtain ten kinds of meritorious benefits in this present life.
First, day and night, one will constantly be protected by the great powerful divine generals of the heavens and their retinues, who remain hidden from view.

Second, one will constantly be followed and protected by twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, as well as all other bodhisattvas. Third, one will constantly be [protected] by all...
The Buddha protects and mindfully remembers them day and night. Amitābha Buddha constantly emits light to gather and sustain this person.

None of the four kinds of evil spirits—whether yakṣas or rākṣasas—can harm them. No venomous snakes or poisonous dragons can harm them at all. Furthermore, they shall not suffer from any of the five calamities:
fires, floods, enemies or bandits, swords and arrows, or imprisonment with shackles and fetters; nor shall they meet with untimely death or unjust death.

1. None of these will be received [as karmic retribution]. 2. All previously committed sins shall be entirely extinguished. 3. The lives of those enemies who were killed shall receive liberation; there will be no further opposition or confrontation. 4.
One’s dreams at night will be upright, or one may dream of Amitābha Buddha’s sublime and wondrous physical body.
5. The mind will be constantly joyful; the complexion will be radiant and lustrous; vital energy will be abundant; and all actions will be auspicious. 6–9. [As stated above.]
They will always be revered, honored, and prostrated to by all the people of the world, just as they would revere a Buddha. Tenth:

at the time of death, their minds shall be free from fear; with right mindfulness manifest before them, they shall behold Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of holy Bodhisattvas, who will hold golden platforms in their hands to welcome them to rebirth in the Western Pure Land, where they shall remain until the end of the future.
Supreme and wondrous bliss. The Buddha strictly forbids people from speaking falsehoods; he would never himself speak falsely to deceive others.
When worldly people speak falsely, it is either to seek profit or to avoid harm. The Buddha has no desires for the world, so how could he seek profit?
The Buddha views birth and death as a sword cutting through empty space; how could he have anything to avoid? Thus, the Buddha has no use for such things.

Regarding this false speech: if you truly believe that the Buddha speaks no falsehoods, you should carefully contemplate these four exhortations for cultivating rebirth in the Pure Land, and you must also rely upon them to encourage others.
Thus, you shall achieve immeasurable merit in both self-deliverance and the deliverance of others. Do not treat this as a mere bookshelf ornament or dismiss it as groundless talk;

do not fail the Buddha’s compassionate heart. For those who lack the karmic affinity for the Buddha and do not believe, I still pray— [The text continues with a plea for compassion toward those who do not believe.]

May you circulate this further and continue to transform and guide one another, so that all may ascend the path to enlightenment wherever they are, and every person may together emerge from the ford of delusion; this is what I hope for you all.

First, an exhortation to those good people who practice mindfulness of the Buddha: In this world there are a thousand paths and ten thousand paths; why do I alone urge people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha?

It is because the human mind is of such profound consequence; it is from this very source that the soul and spirit are led and drawn, and destiny is fashioned and the body brought forth. Nothing arises other than through this.
Contemplating the good leads to rebirth in heaven; contemplating evil leads to entry into hell. Contemplating Māra results in becoming a Māra; contemplating the Buddha results in becoming a Buddha.

This is why people are exhorted to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Among the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, why is it that one is exhorted to recite only the name of Amitābha Buddha?
It is because Amitābha Buddha once made forty-eight vows, each vowing to deliver sentient beings.

Furthermore, because Amitābha Buddha shares a karmic affinity with the sentient beings of this Sahā world, he embraces all who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, whether they be monastics or laypeople, male or female.
Therefore, by single-mindedly holding his name, one will receive his guidance and be reborn in that land.
This refers to evil persons. If they can sincerely repent and hold the Name, they may also attain rebirth while still carrying their karmic burdens.
This is why I urge people to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Nowadays, everyone knows that reciting the Buddha's name is good;

however, because the seeds of karma from greed, anger, ignorance, and attachment accumulated over many lifetimes and kalpas are extremely deep, it is difficult for them to give rise to the resolve [for enlightenment]. All virtuous people, you should know that in this Sahā world...
The realms are filled with extreme suffering and affliction. Observe the people of this world: there are those who are utterly poor and lowly;
those who suffer many calamities and illnesses; those who are widowed, orphaned, or solitary; and those whose spouses are unvirtuous or whose children are unworthy.
Each person has their own realm of suffering, each person has their own circumstances of misery; that such suffering exists goes without saying. Even as for the wealthy...
Those who possess noble health and vigor, whose households are filled with harmony and obedience, who have every necessity fulfilled and all their desires met—these are indeed free from suffering.

Yet, what can be done? One's lifespan is limited. Setting aside those of short life, even if you were to live to a hundred years, when the great destiny arrives, death cannot be avoided. At that moment, one is left with nothing but...
The coffin remains closed forever; all affairs have come to rest. That former splendor—where is it now? When one speaks to this point, it is still nothing but suffering.

As for those who committed evil while alive, after death they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, receiving retribution according to their karma until that evil karma is fully expiated, at which time they may finally regain a human body. This is also true for those who practiced virtue while alive.
It is merely planting the causes for some meritorious retribution. Yet, fearing that the karmic offenses from previous lives may be heavy, one must first settle those debts;
otherwise, upon rebirth, one will inevitably suffer and fall into the three miserable realms.

Even if there were no great transgressions or karma from previous lives and one immediately attains merit in this life, let alone the fact that such fortune can never be complete, even those who receive blessings likewise have their share of suffering.
Even if one were to experience extreme happiness and exhaust all the pleasures of wealth and nobility, one would still return to poverty and lowliness;
how much more so when such wealth and nobility are easily lost through one's actions, inevitably leading one to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals?

To speak not at all of human wealth and nobility, even if one performs the greatest of virtuous deeds and is reborn in the heavens, once the heavenly blessings are exhausted, one will return to the same state.
Falling away is ultimately suffering, for within the three realms there are such places of suffering.

Therefore, out of compassion, our Buddha preached one scroll of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, teaching people to recite the Buddha’s name so that they may attain birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, forever depart from all sufferings, and enjoy happiness eternally.
This was proclaimed directly from the Golden Mouth; since the Buddha does not speak falsehoods, how could he instead speak falsely?
This deceives people. However, human beings are not uniform, and the reasons for failing to resolve to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name (*nienfo*) are likewise diverse.
Some do not recite because they are unaware of the benefits of reciting the Buddha’s name; some do not recite due to a lack of faith;
some do not recite because they are greedily attached to immediate pleasures; and some do not recite because of various obstacles. These differences are manifold. Little do they realize that...
This single invocation of the Buddha's name is something that no one is incapable of recollecting, nor is there anyone who ought not to recollect it.

If one were to insist that the entire world abandon the vocations of scholar, farmer, artisan, and merchant, as well as the various crafts and technical skills, to devote themselves solely to recollecting the Buddha, this would be nothing but obstructing people;

it is certainly not what is meant by "exhortation. For those who practice the recitation of the name, all their ordinary activities are entirely unimpeded; thus, they do not neglect their worldly duties.
Furthermore, it does not squander wealth, nor does it violate the laws of the state; yet it allows one to escape the sufferings of the hells and the cycle of rebirth.

Is this not a matter that is neither beneficial nor harmful to the world, wherein one gains two benefits with a single effort? It is precisely for those who seek tranquility that the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) is most appropriate.
Whether one possesses a stable livelihood at home requiring no further labor, or has parents, elder brothers, younger brothers, or children upon whom one can rely, for oneself—
Those who are at peace and free from affairs have accumulated merit through their past lives; such people are rare to find. It is precisely for them to practice the Way now.
To let one's time pass in vain and spend a lifetime in emptiness would be most regrettable. For those who are busy and distracted, it is precisely the right time to recite the Buddha’s name.
Even if you cannot match those with nothing to do by performing the liturgical recitations during the six periods of the day, you must still recite amidst your busyness.

This is a way to find respite from worldly toil. The *Longshu Jingtuwen* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu) states: "If one recites the ten recitations with a sincere heart every morning, maintaining single-minded devotion and earnest aspiration, one will likewise attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
If one follows this dharma-gate, it is far superior to a lifetime of frantic activity that ultimately results in emptiness."

Those who are wealthy and noble are precisely those who should practice the Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*). Though wealth and nobility may endure for a long time, how can one rely upon a body that is not firm?

Why not take this moment, when everything is already provided, and resolve to practice the Buddha-remembrance? Those who are poor and destitute are precisely those who should practice the Buddha-remembrance.
If you did not cultivate merit in past lives, you suffer poverty in this life; if you do not cultivate it now, after death you will be like a scale-beam falling into a well. What then?

If one can attain liberation even in such circumstances, how much more so through this Dharma-gate of Buddha-recollection? It does not hinder or distract you from seeking clothing or food; since such a skillful means exists, why do you not practice it?
Young people, this is precisely the time to recite the Buddha’s name. While your spirits are strong and robust, seek supreme Bodhi;
as merit accumulates day by day and month by month, its efficacy will never be in vain. Furthermore, human lifespans are not uniform, and there are many who meet with untimely death.

If one can cultivate in secret and, relying on the Buddha’s protection, enjoy a long life, then looking back at those who met an early death, one will finally believe that the application of effort was not in vain.
For the elderly, it is precisely the right time to practice *nianfo*; having passed so many years, perhaps their affairs are still not yet concluded.
In the end, it will never be resolved. Why not, during this finite span of time, strive with urgency to seek rebirth in the Pure Land?
This is truly being able to accomplish what others cannot. Those who have wives and children are precisely the ones who should practice Buddha-recitation.

It is commonly said that "with a son, all matters are sufficient," and it is also said that "sons and grandsons have their own blessings. Such people are exactly those who should set their minds at ease and study the Buddha-dharma.
Yet he remains foolishly attached and refuses to let go, willingly consenting to remain a mere beast of burden for the rest of his life.

He does not consider at all the immense toil and bloodshed expended, imagining it has nothing to do with himself. When the moment of birth and death arrives, even the most filial person cannot take one’s place.
Widowers, widows, orphans, and the solitary—these are precisely the ones who should practice Buddha-recitation. There are many such people, yet they do not come to seek [the Way].
Debtors are not few among men; thus, there is no way to repay it all. Left alone as a solitary individual, one need not worry about sons being married nor daughters being wedded.
Why not take this opportunity to focus the mind single-mindedly on the Western [Pure Land] and leap out of birth and death?
For every fraction of attachment diminished, there is a corresponding reduction in bondage; with every reduction in bondage, there is a reduction in karmic obstructions. As for the world...

Those with shallow karmic conditions will instead have deep karmic conditions with the Buddha; therefore, who can surpass such people? They have no anxiety in life and no attachment or obstruction at death.

Truly, they are the foremost among those in the world who should practice mindfulness of the Buddha—those for whom the effort is half the work while the merit is doubled. It is precisely when one has the bonds of love for wife and concubines that it is most appropriate to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
As the ancients said: "A husband and wife are like birds in the same forest; when the great limit arrives, each must go their own way."
They depart on their own accord. Furthermore, it is said that the affection between flesh and blood is difficult to sustain until white-haired old age;
how much better it would be to cultivate both together for the Land of Ultimate Bliss, so that in the future we may join arms upon the lotus pedestal as Dharma friends for immeasurable kalpas.

Compared to this limited worldly affection, is this not far more excellent? Those whose flesh-and-blood relations harbor resentment should precisely recite the Buddha’s name; even when meeting an enemy, though they may be close, [the bond is fleeting].

Do not be intimate with them; do not fail to explain the truth early on, lest their bonds become ever more deeply entangled. If you constantly recite the name of Amitābha, you shall attain liberation in this very life.
Women, you should especially practice mindfulness of the Buddha, for by nature a woman’s body is one of the five outflows and a fallen state.
I am truly distressed that I cannot escape [suffering]. Having obtained this Dharma-door of Buddha-remembrance so easily, why do you not yet practice with urgency to leave the realms of suffering?
Furthermore, among the forty-eight vows made by Amitābha Buddha, the thirty-fifth vow states:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be women in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions..."

If anyone, upon hearing my name, rejoices with faith and delight, resolves to attain Bodhicitta, and feels revulsion toward the female body, yet after the end of their life is reborn again in a female form, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Because these women have exclusively cultivated the Pure Land, they will surely be able to escape the female body and realize the fruit of Bodhi;
however, they must not fail to practice mindfulness of the Buddha by being deluded by false views. [Regarding] those with physical disabilities:

A human being ought to practice the Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*). If one’s physical faculties and characteristics are already incomplete, it is difficult to compare them with those of ordinary people;

were they to fall further, they would inevitably enter the three miserable realms (*trāya*), where the suffering would be even more intense. A person afflicted by illness ought to practice the Buddha-remembrance.

Even those who are robust must guard against sudden death, let alone one whose very condition is a cause for death. Even if one does not immediately die, one is perpetually entangled in the continuous suffering of sickness. It is just like this:

In the Reviving Hell (*saṃjīva*), practice with urgency; even then, fear that it may be too late. Those who encounter calamities and disasters are precisely those for whom it is right to recite the Buddha’s name.

When the karma of past lives has ripened, one cannot avoid it in this life; rely entirely upon the Buddha’s power to escape such misfortune. Good people are precisely those for whom it is right to recite the Buddha’s name.
Good people are protected by the Buddha, and their recitation will be even more effective. If one merely performs good deeds without reciting the Buddha’s name, when compared—
As for those who do not perform good deeds, though they may surpass others in worldly awareness, they will receive nothing more than a modicum of stubborn fortune in this life and the next;

once that fortune is exhausted, they must inevitably fall. It is better, therefore, to practice virtue and further recite the Buddha’s name, so as to be reborn directly in the highest grade of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where there shall never again be a time of falling.
For the wicked person, it is precisely the right time to recite the Buddha’s name; while committing evil brings punishment, the people of the world [should instead seek liberation].
Everyone knows this, yet it is simply because you have never examined yourself. Now that you have awakened at the fifth watch, reflect upon each thing one by one.
If they are indeed evil, seek repentance immediately; reform your wickedness and follow the good, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.

The Buddha is greatly compassionate and there is none whom He will not deliver. Thus, examine your life: there is no evil you have not committed, and perhaps past transgressions have already formed great obstacles to your progress.
There is no hope of salvation even by a ten-thousandth part. In some cases, within the present circumstances, one finds it as difficult to dismount from a tiger as it is to retreat;
one can only harden one's heart. Or there are prostitutes and litigants who scheme for the wealth and lives of many; or butchers and fishermen who harm billions of living beings.
If one judges the cause by its effect, they ought to receive the retribution of intense suffering for long kalpas, from which there is no rescue or aid. Nevertheless, one must absolutely not—
Self-destructive and self-abandoning, you seek only the present, passing each day as best you can.

You must know that the Buddha opened the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha precisely out of compassion for sentient beings such as yourselves who are destined to undergo suffering; he sought to uproot your extreme agony and lead you to Ultimate Bliss.
Although you have committed these great dark karmas, that you are able to encounter the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha and rebirth there is due to the accumulated merit of many lifetimes.
This is a most extraordinary and great auspicious condition, a supreme act of destiny. You must urgently seize this opportunity before the retribution of suffering arrives;
resolve with fierce diligence to recite the Buddha’s name, relying steadfastly upon this single thought to perfect the power of the vow for certain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Seek out virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) who can provide instruction and discourse to further increase your faith. Observe those such as the eminent monks Xunjun and Zhang Shanhe from the past;
they serve as prime examples of those who attained rebirth despite being extremely wicked. Do this early, do it early! Do not doubt, do not doubt!

Apart from this single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha, there is no other more direct method for salvation. Those who practice the meditative concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) are precisely those who should practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

There is a class of people who are attached to stillness and concentration, believing that when not a single thought arises and they have "put it down again and again," they may attain a state of emptiness for a day or two, and then claim, "This is the Great Vajra Samādhi. Thus, they become fixated upon it.

Do not abandon it. Since this does not accord with the path of the Chan school, and you do not know how to investigate the teachings or contemplate the mind, how could you realize that even after eighty thousand kalpas, one will ultimately fall into emptiness and oblivion?
It would be better to recite the Buddha’s name morning and evening and dedicate the merit toward the Western Pure Land;

this will by no means hinder meditative concentration, nor will it obstruct rebirth there. It is a thousandfold secure and ten-thousandfold certain—is this not excellent? This applies to those who recite sutras and dharanis as well.
This is precisely the time to practice nianfo (recitation of the Buddha’s name). One must simply recite with a sincere heart; it must not be treated as a mere ritual formality.

Whether reciting the Buddha’s name or chanting sutras, one must dedicate the merit toward rebirth in the Western Pure Land, and one will certainly attain rebirth there. For those who practice Chan meditation, this is also the proper time to practice nianfo.

Having attained great enlightenment through Chan and having seen through birth and death, they have already recognized Amitābha within their own nature (*svabhāva*). However, when practice and understanding are in accord, it is called [the perfection of both].
The Patriarch [Huineng] said: "Therefore, even the Second Patriarch still had to 'tune his own mind,' and even the Sixth Patriarch still spoke of 'saving oneself at the moment of awakening.

It is precisely appropriate to cultivate with constant and subtle diligence. One must by no means harbor deluded views and slander the Pure Land. Do not say that when birth and death arrive, one cannot be the master;
for even if one could attain freedom from birth and death, if there is the slightest trace of attachment or lingering thought, it will be difficult to avoid the three [sufferings]."

When the causes of past karma ripen and the realms of the five aggregates manifest before one, one may slip away in an instant, continuing as before to leak back into the cycle of saṃsāra. How lamentable!

Truly lamentable! A hundred errors, a thousand errors, and ten thousand errors—how much better it would be to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, for then every practice leads to that destination.

Those who lecture on the teachings should especially recite the Buddha’s name; for although the thousands of sutras and myriad treatises open various gates of practice, [it is this which is most essential].

They differ. In all cases, one must completely eradicate both the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) before one can escape the cycle of saṃsāra. However, how easy is this to talk about?

Setting aside for a moment the various schools of India—such as those of Nature (*svabhāva*), Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and Esotericism (*guhya*)—even within this land [of China], among the three traditions of Tiantai, Xianshou, and Weishi, none consider the severing of the delusions of views and thought to be anything other than the stage of transcending birth and death. This...
Regarding the stage where the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*) are severed: for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, this constitutes the rank of an Arhat of the fourth fruit;

for those of the Perfect Vehicle (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), it constitutes a partial realization corresponding to the stage of semblance. Since the Buddha-dharma flowed eastward, how many people have been able to reach this level?

Furthermore, as the sutras and śāstras frequently praise rebirth [in the Pure Land], one should resolutely and vigorously practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), following the teachings in practice. —The Path of the Nuns.

Mother-in-law, it is precisely now that you should practice the Buddha-recitation. You currently dwell in the ground of Buddhahood within this pure place of practice. Recite the Buddha’s name with sincere devotion morning and evening;
cultivate liberation for yourself and serve as an example for the world. If you thus truly seek rebirth in the Pure Land, your merit will be infinitely greater than that of others.
Why is this? Because the women of the world often rely on your guidance and instruction. Thus it is said:
If one can exhort others toward the true path of Buddha-recitation, not merely seeking one's own salvation but also being capable of delivering others—how could such merit not be magnificent?
Even external acts of giving will then arrive spontaneously without being sought.

If, however, one uses Buddha-recitation as a pretext for soliciting donations, or for establishing "life-extension" funds and "posthumous money" for the underworld after death, these are all heterodox doctrines that deceive people; they are not [the true practice].
To mistakenly lead others is simply to mistake oneself. All that has been stated above follows the bequeathed teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

it is not a fabrication from thin air. I only wish that those who see and hear this will each admonish their own minds. One must know that the Sahā world is truly suffering, while the Western Land is truly blissful.
The suffering of the Sahā world involves an unceasing cycle of rebirth, whereas the bliss of the Western Land endures for immeasurable kalpas. Be earnest!

Do not say that one who does not know suffering cannot speak of it; for while speaking of suffering is easy, actually undergoing suffering is real and difficult. Even the slightest suffering is already felt as hard to bear, let alone intense suffering.
One must not refuse to hear of happiness or disbelieve in happiness. If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what else can be believed?
Even when a person in this world who is loyal, trustworthy, and honest speaks a single word, others do not doubt them; how much more so, then, with the Buddha?
He said: "Excellent, excellent! Hurry and quickly turn back; resolve your mind to recite the Buddha's name.
Second, I exhort all virtuous people to recite the Buddha's name with sincerity:
now that you have resolved to recite the Buddha's name, you must do so with a sincere heart; it must not be merely in name without substance."
Indeed. Generally speaking, those who lack roots of goodness can never truly practice the Buddha-recitation. Thus, the ancients said: "To hear the Buddha-dharma is difficult;
to have true faith is even more difficult. That you are now able to resolve to recite the Buddha’s name is a root of goodness that must be cultivated and increased at every moment;

you must not deceive yourself. As for those who practice Buddha-recitation while also being proficient in both the Exoteric (Shu) and Esoteric (Zong) teachings, regarding the aspects of phenomena (shi) and principle (li):
The two are fused: one neither clings to principle while abandoning phenomena, nor perceives principle apart from phenomena.

Such persons have a clear understanding, free from doubt, regarding all teachings on the single mind in phenomena and the single mind in principle; they can be certain of their rebirth in the highest grade of the upper realm and being welcomed by the golden platform.
There is no need for others to offer further exhortation or praise, nor do I require any superfluous words here. Now, simply maintain mindfulness toward the side of phenomena.
Regarding the Buddha, there are three grades. As for the first grade: their faith is sincere and earnest; they practice with utmost integrity, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name.
Although they engage in the ordinary activities of dressing and eating, they believe in this one matter alone.
Walking, they are Amitābha; sitting, they are Amitābha. Even if they are as busy as an arrow, they do not depart from Amitābha. This is the essence.
Advancing without retreating: today it is thus, tomorrow it will be thus; this year it is thus, next year it will be thus.
Such people as these the Buddha will certainly protect and guide, and on the day their lives end, they will surely be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
As for those of the second grade, their minds may not be single-minded; although they also know the benefits of reciting the Buddha’s name, worldly thoughts are heavy.
Right mindfulness is light. When you are reciting the Buddha’s name, your mind thinks of other matters;

or it is like "one day of heat followed by ten days of cold"—you might practice for one day and then be separated from it for ten. If you recite the Buddha’s name in such a manner, even if you continue until old age, it will be of no avail;
it will merely plant a root of goodness. In a future life, when conditions meet, you may be touched by this small root of goodness and [awaken].
One must practice with sincerity; only then can one hope for accomplishment. As for those of the third grade, they recite with their mouths but do not recite with their minds.
They originally do not know the benefits of reciting the Buddha’s name, but merely seek the reputation of being a practitioner.
Today they join the procession at this Buddhist assembly and recite for a day; tomorrow they join the procession at that Buddhist assembly and recite for a day.
To recite the Buddha’s name for a single day—though it is called "reciting the Buddha's name for a day"—in reality, it is merely a waste of time.
One spends more time engaging in idle chatter than one does in reciting the Buddha’s name. While inside the Buddha hall, one still harbors the hearts of greed, anger, delusion, and attachment;
yet once outside the Buddha hall, one cannot avoid the affairs of greed, anger, delusion, and attachment. This is even worse than the second grade.
There are many more. Among these three classes of people, the first class is the smallest, and the third class is also not very numerous.

It is only the second class that everyone easily falls into. This is because the sentient beings of this Sahā world are obscured by material desires and find it difficult to eliminate deluded thoughts;
therefore, it is so. Try to reflect on all worldly affairs: even when one is able to focus one's mind exclusively upon them, [one still falters].

Do not let the mind be distracted by anything else; even to the point where the eyes do not perceive forms, the ears do not perceive sounds, the nose does not perceive fragrances, the tongue does not perceive tastes, and the body does not perceive tactile sensations. Practice continuously, day and night.
This is what it means for the application of the mind to be sincere. Reciting the Buddha’s name must be like this in order to gain efficacy. It is truly as you have said.
To lazily recite the Dharma, though one may plant a single point of wholesome roots, I fear that the roots of evil are deep while the wholesome roots are shallow.
Even if one is free from evil karma in this present life, there is no guarantee that you will not commit evil in future lives; for evil will eventually overwhelm the wholesome.
Although the roots of goodness have been planted, they are difficult to bring forth. Furthermore, one does not know how many kalpas or births it will take before one finally emerges;
is this not a great suffering? One must urgently give rise to a heart of earnest sincerity and exert courageous power. Whatever worldly conditions can be relinquished, relinquish them immediately.
Life is impermanent; do not allow yourself to be deluded by lingering attachment. Even though there may be things that cannot be relinquished, [one must still strive].

This does not obstruct your mindfulness of the Buddha. For example, suppose you have one urgent matter constantly in mind; even while attending to other affairs, would you ever be willing to forget that one urgent matter?

If you can practice mindfulness of the Buddha in this way, distracting thoughts will naturally cease, and you will avoid the fault of practicing with intensity for a day followed by neglect for ten days.
This refers to those whose resolve is not sincere; yet there are also those whose resolve is profoundly sincere.
Yet they are disturbed by demonic influences and cannot attain freedom. They truly know and have profound faith in the merits and benefits of reciting the Buddha’s name;
they have heard much and seen extensively regarding the methods of recitation. However, as for the actual practice of recitation, they are unable to carry it out sufficiently.
When speaking to others, they say that the mind must be single-minded, yet their own practice remains distracted.
While his own mindfulness is unceasing, he speaks to others of courageous diligence, yet he himself is often indolent.

While he speaks to others of the pressing nature of birth and death, he himself is leisurely and indifferent. While he speaks to others of various skillful means, he himself forgets his own self for the sake of others.
What is the reason for this? It is because this person has planted roots of goodness in past lives and in this present life.

Because the mind was clear, he was able to gain a slight, rough understanding and shallow insight. Yet, due to the depth of his past transgressions and the heaviness of his karma, he was thus disturbed by demons.
There are inner demons and outer demons; the inner demon is that which causes the mind to be sometimes awake and sometimes deluded.
All greed, hatred, delusion, and craving—once this mind has just departed, that mind arises again. External demons are the obstacles of adverse circumstances;
various hindering conditions oppress the body and mind, preventing peace and stability.

If one unfortunately encounters such a demonic head, one should immediately make vows before the Buddha and diligently seek repentance to eliminate past transgressions. Among practitioners of antiquity, all...
This matter is indeed a crucial point: it lies in the mind of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name). Do not let this resolve waver because of demonic interference;

establish this will with such firm determination that you do not turn back despite a hundred setbacks. Regardless of whatever obstacles or conditions may arise, let this single invocation of the Buddha’s name never depart from your heart.
Although the power of demonic forces may be strong, rely upon this great name of ten thousand virtues to confront them. Disregarding profit or harm, life or death, simply continue to recite:
recite the six characters, recite the four characters; recite aloud, recite in a low voice; recite clearly or recite silently.
Mindfulness while walking; mindfulness while prostrating; mindfulness while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; mindfulness in moments of tranquility; mindfulness even in times of turmoil;
mindfulness during joy; mindfulness even during affliction; mindfulness in clarity; mindfulness even in dullness; mindfulness even within dreams. One contemplates until the heart is moved to tears;
one contemplates until the fire is extinguished and the ashes grow cold; one contemplates until gods revere and ghosts respect; one contemplates until Heaven rejoices and Māras flee.

A single utterance of "Buddha" eliminates the karmic obstructions of ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes. A single utterance of "Buddha" opens the causal conditions for the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence.
This is truly like pressing oil from seeds; the sound of the striking blows grows increasingly fierce as the boat encounters rising waves.

The sound of rowing the oars grows increasingly mournful. The cauldrons of boiling water lie behind, while the lotus pond lies ahead. Though there may be thousands upon ten thousands of people obstructing my way, [I press on].
Do not harbor such thoughts; vow never to regress. After a long, long time, you will surely receive the Buddha’s compassionate, hidden assistance.
Obstructing conditions will dissolve, and pure conditions will be fulfilled. The Buddha does not fail those who rely on him; he will surely fulfill your aspirations.

Such is the case for those virtuous people with heavy karmic obstructions; those with light obstructions can be understood by analogy. Those with obstructions are like this; those without obstructions can be understood even more so.
Excellent, excellent! Each of you should strive diligently and recite the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart.
I have thrice exhorted all virtuous people to seek rebirth in the Pure Land;
now that you have already recited the Buddha’s name with sincerity, you must resolve to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. You must not seek it in vain.
"Merit and reward. When people of the world hear these words, they cannot help but be greatly startled and alarmed. They think that practicing cultivation is originally for the sake of seeking merit;
that by reciting the Buddha's name one obtains merit is precisely a matter that accords with their hearts' desires and satisfies them. Why, then, would they refuse merit and reward?
If you speak of the Pure Land, how could we ordinary beings be reborn there? Moreover, our spiritual practice is shallow and meager; how could it be permitted?

It is easy for virtuous people to be reborn [in higher realms]. Such a notion is a great error. One must know that the retribution of blessings is subject to exhaustion. Observe the people of this world:
some have wealthy and noble ancestors, yet their descendants are poor and lowly; others were wealthy and noble in their youth, yet impoverished and lowly in their old age.
Is this not proof that the retribution of blessings has its limit? Not only this, but even the practice cultivated in this life may not persist into the next.
They receive blessings, yet fail to cultivate merit in two lifetimes; consequently, they suffer again in the third.

Some, having exhausted their retribution as animals, barely attain human form, but with their human capacity impaired, they fall back into the animal realm; thus their ascent and descent are unstable, which is why this is called floating and sinking in the sea of suffering.
Not only this: some have wealth but no children; some have children but no wealth; some have longevity but are solitary and destitute.
Some are intelligent yet short-lived; some are wealthy yet foolish and dull-witted; some are noble yet invite calamity; some are free from personal ailment yet suffer the loss of their kin;
others have their households relatively at peace yet are themselves afflicted by chronic illness. Because one thing is always missing another, it is called the "World of Deficiencies.
Do you think that karmic rewards are always in accordance with one's heart's desires? If one is born in the Western Land...
It is not so. They are born by transformation within lotus flowers; their bodies are fragrant and pure, their features are upright and handsome, and their minds possess wisdom free from afflictions.
Food and clothing appear spontaneously; they are without sickness or old age, and they follow the Buddha with sovereign ease, dwelling in leisure and peace at An-yang (Sukhāvatī).
The lifespan of such persons is likewise immeasurable, and from this state they proceed directly to the path of Buddhahood, never again to fall back. As for other types of birth...
The various forms of happiness therein cannot be fully described; all were spoken directly from the Buddha’s own mouth, as seen in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and other Mahāyāna sūtras.
From this perspective, human wealth and status vanish into emptiness in the blink of an eye, whereas the bliss of the Western Land remains eternal.
It is inexhaustible and endless. Why, then, do you not urgently make vows to seek rebirth?

If you say, "I am but an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and I fear I cannot attain rebirth," you must know that our Buddha, the Tathāgata, specifically intended this for us ordinary people whose obstructions are deep and wisdom shallow.
If one practices other methods, they all involve exiting the triple world through vertical progression; I fear such paths may not allow one to achieve liberation within a single lifetime.

[One will] die. For this reason, the single practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) has been specially opened up, with the wish that people may attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], thereby fulfilling the vow to save all sentient beings to the end.
Why do you thus abandon yourself, failing to think of self-exertion and betraying the boundless compassion of our Buddha?

If you consider your own merit and practice to be shallow, you must know that the great name of the Buddha, endowed with myriad virtues, does not fail to encompass any goodness. There is nothing it does not include...
Evil is not extinguished; this is precisely a practice that is most great, most profound, most vast, and most perfect.
Therefore, a single recitation of the Buddha’s name can extinguish immeasurable heavy sins accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

One must not regard the recitation of the Buddha’s name as trivial or mundane, lest one treat it with contempt in the future. Furthermore, one must know that those who recite the Buddha’s name rely entirely upon Amitābha Buddha.
Gathered by the power of the Great Compassionate Vow, when Amitābha Buddha first made his forty-eight vows, each vow was intended to deliver sentient beings.

The eighteenth vow states: "When I attain Buddhahood, if those among the devas and humans in the countless worlds of the ten directions should, with a sincere heart of faith and joy, desire to be born in my land and recite my name ten times, they shall surely come to be born there. Only...
Except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the true Dharma, they shall not obtain this vow and shall never become Buddhas.
Because the Buddha possesses this great vow, one who single-mindedly recites the name of Amitābha Buddha shall have a lotus flower immediately produced within the Western Seven-Jeweled Pond,
inscribed with that person’s name as a marker, so that they may take rebirth therein on a future day at the moment their life ends.
At that time, Amitābha Buddha, together with the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, manifests his form to welcome and guide them.
From antiquity to the present, those who have attained rebirth there are beyond counting. Some individuals know in advance the date of their death;
when that time arrives, they themselves declare that they see the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, and thus pass away peacefully. In other cases, bystanders likewise witness auspicious omens.
Radiance. Hearing the same fragrant scents and the distinct sounds of drums and music—none of which are vague or indistinct—is recorded in all the biographies of those who attained rebirth.

Today, however, those whose recitation of the Buddha’s name is sincere are few; therefore, those who attain rebirth are not many. Because people see such instances rarely, they do not possess full deep faith.
Little do they realize that there is one person every thousand *li* and one person every hundred *li*. These thousands of *li*...
When Baili attained rebirth, was he alone not an ordinary person? One person in ten years;

one person in five years—were those who attained rebirth during these ten or five-year intervals alone not ordinary persons? Do all of these who attain rebirth possess the meritorious practices of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*?
They are nothing more than being able to apply their minds with sincere earnestness. This is clearly stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

If there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, uphold his name for one day, or even up to seven days, with single-mindedness and without distraction, they shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This is entirely due to the great vows and great power of Amitābha Buddha. It is like a great ship: whatever object it may be, as long as it boards [the ship]...
A boat will surely reach the other shore and one need not fear sinking; therefore, the ancients said:
"Studying the Way through other gates is like an ant climbing a high mountain, whereas seeking rebirth by reciting the Buddha's name is like a wind-blown sail traveling downstream.
When a boat travels downstream and encounters a favorable wind, how joyful and swift it is! This is precisely the principle of relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows."
"O virtuous people, 'following the current and the wind' refers to what happens after one has already boarded the boat. Suppose you are unwilling to board; what will you do then?
Therefore, one must still possess a sincere and earnest power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). As for those who practice the Buddha-recitation (*buddhānusmṛti*) today..."
Some resolve their minds out of the suffering of illness; some for the protection of their households; some for the elimination of calamities and the prolongation of life in the present;
and some falsely seek wealth and status for future lives. Few are those who, regarding the great matter of birth and death, resolve to be born in the Pure Land.

It is like a person traveling south or north: they must have a predetermined direction. If one has predetermined to go south, then at the moment of stepping out the door, [one must proceed accordingly].
One does not depart from the north. If you do not now make a vow to seek the Pure Land, how will you be able to go there when your life comes to an end?
This refers to those who do not make a vow to seek rebirth; furthermore, their vows may lack sincerity and earnestness.
Though they say with their mouths that they wish to be born in the West, their hearts are constantly attached to worldly desires. Even if they occasionally give rise to the aspiration...
The aspiration for rebirth cannot, in general, be maintained as a single day throughout one's entire life.
While it is certainly good to attain rebirth, if it does not occur, then there is no practical benefit at all; it remains the same as if no aspiration had been made. Alas!
The sentient beings of this defiled age crave worldly splendor and willingly sink into degradation, seeking no liberation. Truly, there is nothing that can be done for them. In sum:

The Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance is inconceivable; the bliss of the Western Land is beyond compare. To practice Buddha-remembrance and seek rebirth therein perfectly accords with the Buddha’s own heart.
If you wish to be born there, you shall be born; if you do not wish it, you will not. If your vow is not earnest and focused, it is the same as having no vow at all.
It is not that the Buddha does not deliver you, but rather that you lack a resolute will. If, by means of this inconceivable Dharma-gate, you go to seek worldly things...
There is a limit to the karmic reward of such merit. It would be as lamentable as using a bright pearl to strike at a sparrow. Excellent, excellent!
One should sincerely make vows to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.

Fourth, exhorting all virtuous people to cultivate both the primary and auxiliary practices together: Since you now seek rebirth in the Pure Land, you must cultivate both the primary and auxiliary practices so that you may attain rebirth at the end of life.

Not only does this ensure certainty and freedom from doubt, but it also elevates one's spiritual rank. Although there are many gateways to correct cultivation, the single method of upholding the Name is paramount.
This is because upholding the Name is easy, and the merit gained is likewise easy to attain. Regarding this primary practice of upholding the Name, the ancient masters have said:
This opens the three gates of faith, practice, and aspiration. The meaning of the preceding section has already been briefly set forth; here, four further points shall be elaborated.
May those with resolve study them and put them into practice. First: Have firm faith in the Buddha’s words.

Consider that since beginningless time, you have transmigrated through the six realms of existence without liberation. By what good fortune have you now given rise to this mind for transcendence? Furthermore—
Fortunately, you have been able to hear the method of rebirth through *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), which is most easy and most swift;
yet you still hesitate and remain undecided. This ailment arises solely because your faith in the Buddha has not been truly sincere. You must understand this:

are there any who surpass the Buddha in wisdom, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), insight, power, supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), compassion, or ascetic practice? Thus, that which the Buddha has taught—
The Dharma cuts through errors and does not lead people astray; for this reason, the Buddha’s words are called true speech, reality-based speech, and non-deceptive speech.
The Buddha taught that even an extremely evil person, if they achieve ten recitations at the moment of death, shall also attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Throughout your entire life, your conduct may not have been free from extreme evil; yet, the number of times you have recited the Name likely exceeds ten recitations.
If you were nonetheless unable to attain rebirth in the Pure Land, it would mean that the Buddha had misled people and led them down a wrong path—how could such a thing possibly be true?
Now, you need only believe with sincerity, maintain single-minded devotion in every thought, and practice daily without fail until the moment of your death.
If one maintains mindfulness with the sincere desire for rebirth, there will be no error whatsoever; one will certainly attain rebirth without doubt.

It is like planting melon seeds and inevitably obtaining melons, or planting bean seeds and inevitably obtaining beans. It is also like using a sun-mirror to produce fire or a magnet to attract a needle:
provided that the conditions and the response coincide, there is absolutely nothing that will not be efficacious. One must by no means create obstacles for oneself or falter in progress. Its...

If there are those whose doubts are deep and heavy such that, despite hearing these teachings, they remain inwardly unsettled by indecision, this is due to the stubbornness of their karmic obstructions.
They must constantly maintain right mindfulness and further apply themselves to repentance morning and evening;
as months and years pass, their faculty of wisdom will naturally be revealed, and through sincere faith free from doubt, their practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) will become perfect.
"Power has been gained. This constitutes the first essential point for initiating right practice and engendering faith. Second, one must personally rely upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Although the practice of *buddhānusmṛti* (mindfulness of the Buddha) is an extremely easy matter, if one does not gain power through it, one will realize after a long time that there is no benefit whatsoever.

When encountering circumstances that are unfavorable, one may easily give rise to regression and indolence; or, upon hearing teachings on various dharmas of dhyāna and contemplation, one might think to practice Chan meditation or cultivate observation, thereby changing from one method to another.
Without relying upon an enlightened teacher and virtuous friends to provide exhortation and critical evaluation, one will certainly not be free from considerable errors.
Therefore, although cultivation requires personal exertion, it entirely depends upon the power of spiritual mentors. As the Sūtra says:
A virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the complete causal condition for attaining the Way. Suppose one’s own practice has gone astray;

it is by relying on the guidance of a virtuous friend that one returns to the correct path. Suppose one’s own practice has become lax; it is by relying on the virtuous friend’s admonition and encouragement that one is revitalized.
That which I do not know, I hope the virtuous friend will explain; that which I already know, I require the virtuous friend to certify. If...
Those who have mastered both the language and the meaning should, at this time, study the scriptural teachings to increase their roots of faith in the Pure Land.

Furthermore, they must discuss and investigate them with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); only then can they avoid the error of becoming mired in literal interpretations that lead to self-deception.

Master Sheng'an said: "In this world, even for minor arts, one cannot do without teachers and friends; how much more so for the practice of *nianfo*, which is a dharma-gate for transcending birth and death? If one lacks knowledge..."
From what does consciousness develop? Who acts as its guide? A single moment of non-awakening leads to a fall; the error committed is no small matter.
When the time of death arrives, a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) becomes even more essential. Master Shandao said:

"When an ordinary person’s life comes to an end and they wish to be born in the Pure Land, they must not fear death. They should constantly reflect that this body is full of suffering, impurity, and evil karma."

Amidst these various entanglements, if you can cast off this defiled body, you will transcend to birth in a Pure Land and experience immeasurable bliss, being liberated from the miserable realms of birth and death as easily as discarding tattered clothing to put on precious garments. You should let go of both body and mind and harbor no lingering attachments.
Whenever you encounter illness, contemplate impermanence; with single-minded devotion, recite the Buddha’s name while awaiting death. You may then entrust your family members with these instructions.
Furthermore, those who attend to the dying person should recite the Buddha's name for them and must not speak of trivial or worldly matters at hand.
At the moment of death, relatives must not shed tears or wail, nor should they utter sounds of lamentation or distress, as these will disturb and confuse the mind.
If one loses right mindfulness, others should at once chant the Buddha’s name with a single voice to assist them in rebirth in the Pure Land.
One may only weep mournfully once the body has grown cold; if there is even the slightest attachment to this world, it will become an obstacle, and liberation will not be attained.
It would be a source of great fortune if those who clearly understand the Pure Land were to come frequently to exhort and encourage the dying. Whenever I observe the people of this world...
At that time, one recollects the Buddha and seeks rebirth in the Western Land; yet, when facing illness, one again fears death and fails to speak of the matter of rebirth and liberation.
The threshold of death is a momentous affair; one must exert effort for oneself. Observing such instructions as those of Master Shandao, one can know that this is a vital and crucial point.
First, one must draw near to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); only then will one obtain their guidance at the time of death.
This is assisted by power. This constitutes a vital point for the cultivation of right practice through exhortation. Third, one should constantly apply diligence.
There are many forms of diligence, such as the daily liturgical practices and the method of ten recitations listed below.

Alternatively, one may limit the number of Buddha-names recited each day, according to each person’s own assessment of their busyness or leisure, establishing a fixed schedule that continues for the duration of this present life without interruption for even a single day; this is called constant diligence.

When encountering times of leisure, one may set a specific period—such as a full day and night, up to seven days, twenty-one days, or forty-nine days—to focus one's mindfulness exclusively upon the practice.
With the aim of swiftly realizing samādhi, this is called courageous diligence. Regarding the method of mindfulness of the Buddha:

whether one person or many people are reciting, whether reciting while sitting cross-legged or walking, and whether holding the name silently or aloud, one must always rely single-mindedly on the Buddha’s name.

Each syllable must be distinct; if it becomes indistinct, one must immediately arouse alert observation. Should the mind fall into a state of non-discrimination (*avyākṛta*), one must likewise rectify it.

If the mind flows into discursive thoughts, immediately awaken it and pull it back. Use this single phrase of the Buddha’s name to permeate and constrain the mental faculty (*manas*), thereby blocking both paths of miscellaneous thoughts and dullness.
This is the correct and thorough method of *nien-fo*. It must not be too hurried; if hurried, it will be difficult to sustain for long.
It must not be too slow; if slow, it will easily dissipate. Furthermore, one must not hope to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*), nor should one entirely refrain from applying the mind.
If you let go of the practice and recite merely as the words come to you, it is easiest to fall into a state of light drowsiness.
For the essence of Buddha-recitation lies in single-mindedness without distraction. At the moment of death, one relies entirely upon this very thought to enter directly into the lotus womb;

this is something practitioners of Buddha-recitation must understand. When one reaches the ultimate state of single-mindedness, meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) will manifest spontaneously, without being sought.
This is the stage when one's practice has reached maturity; it is utterly different from those who, having let go, fall into a state of casual, dull-mindedness.
Delve into this again and again until you reach the point of thorough investigation: thought is itself non-thought, and it is perfectly permissible to think within the state of non-thought.
This single thought-moment is precisely the three truths of emptiness, conventionality, and the middle; it is precisely the four dharma-realms of phenomena and principle;
it is precisely the two contemplations of consciousness-only and mind-only; it is precisely the true mark, the signless, the wondrous mind of nirvana.

This is the method for those of superior faculties who contemplate the Dharma with a single-minded focus on principle. Nevertheless, one must not depart from relying on the Buddha’s name within this single mind, reciting it with every syllable clearly distinct.
This is one of the most essential points regarding the rules for the correct practice of reciting the name. Fourth, one must diligently and earnestly maintain mindfulness.
To seek rebirth in the Pure Land by means of the merit of this Buddha-recitation is the vow; however, one must constantly and sincerely offer such prayers.

One should rejoice in and dedicate all merit toward goodness, and repent of and dedicate all evil. At all times and in all matters, there should be no occasion when one does not aspire to the Western Land;
thus, the conditions for the Pure Land will ripen, and at the moment of death, one will be reborn there as easily as traveling on a light carriage along a familiar road, without any hindrance.
Furthermore, the visualization of Amitābha is especially essential for the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Chapter on Mahāsthāmaprāpta: By recollecting the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future. "Recollecting" means binding the mind to all matters;
that is, recollecting the adornments of Amitābha’s environment and its inhabitants, or visualizing the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, and the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies.

As well as the white tuft between the brows, the hands hanging down, the halo, the emanated Buddhas, the lotus flowers, and other such signs. Alternatively, one may recollect the compassionate vows and meritorious virtues of Amitābha:

for "the single mind" refers to the concentration of one's focus upon a single object. It is like those who plot for wealth or lust after beauty:
all their spirits, souls, and myriad calculations are consolidated into a single undertaking, with the sole aim of securing their prize.
Only then does it cease; thus, one cannot help but call this "single-mindedness. Therefore, a practitioner of Buddha-remembrance must never forget the Buddha even in moments of haste or distraction.

After a long time, this becomes their nature, and they will spontaneously and constantly recollect Him. This can obstruct all evil thoughts and bring to fruition all pure causes and meritorious virtues.
As an ancient master’s verse says: "If at the moment of death one is unable to contemplate or recite, simply generate the thought:"

This is the fundamental duty of a practitioner; yet among worldly people, those who are negligent in the mindfulness of the Buddha are many.

The practitioner regards a paper image or a wooden statue as identical to the true Buddha. Loving them as one's own parents and honoring them as a sovereign, they attend to them morning and evening with absolute sincerity and reverence.
They prostrate themselves like a mountain collapsing and rise like clouds ascending; upon emerging, they offer their greetings.

When people inquire after one another’s well-being, whether from a hundred or a thousand *li* away, they should always feel as if the person were before their eyes. Before partaking of even a single drink or a morsel of food, one must first offer it in service.

"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall first deliver these classes of sentient beings. Through this compassionate heart, may their past karma be extinguished.

among those currently practicing for the Pure Land, some may fall short of me and others may surpass me.
As for those who fall short, you must by no means compare yourself to them and claim that you are superior. If you do so, there will be no further progress.

"He is a man of noble character, and I am likewise so. If I do not rouse my spirit to become a hero, I shall watch him soar high to the Land of Ultimate Bliss while I continue to drift and sink in the sea of suffering.
Those whom I now call friends and fellow practitioners are pleasant to associate with in speech and laughter;

yet in the blink of an eye, they will be separated as the holy from the mundane, a distance as vast as that between heaven and earth. Am I not ashamed? Am I not sorrowful? Reflecting thus, one [should awaken].

Nevertheless, one must press forward with courage and accomplish the task within this single lifetime, without waiting for future lives. Among practitioners today, there are those who vow to practice again in a future life;
according to their own assessment, they claim that their merit and practice in this life are too shallow, and that only by adding further effort in the next life can they hope for success.
This is truly a great error. As the sutra says: "Once one loses this human body..."

Furthermore, according to what he says—that by making a vow in this life, one will surely know how to practice in a future life through the power of that vow—this too is an error.
Since such power is gained by making a vow, why not instead vow to be born in the Pure Land in this very life? Then you will naturally and certainly attain it.
Rebirth in the Pure Land—why must you wait for a future life? Moreover, if you do not seek rebirth in this present life, will you be able to seek it in the next?

Should you encounter other obstructive conditions in a future life and cease your practice, not only would you fail to attain rebirth, but you might even lose your human form altogether. Thus, the ancients said: "If you do not [attain enlightenment] in this body..."
One must now attain liberation in this very life; toward what other birth could one hope to deliver this body? Those who recite the Buddha’s name must resolutely establish this vow:

they should view their current dwelling in the Sahā world as merely a temporary lodging, and they must regard themselves as inhabitants of the Pure Land, whose spiritual station is of the highest excellence.
Thus, they will naturally practice with constant and diligent vigor until they have attained the fruit of realization, at which point they shall finally cease. This is especially so...
This is one essential method for attaining rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus far, the six auxiliary practices have been briefly explained in this manner.
Were they to be explained in detail, they would comprise ten thousand practices; it is up to each individual to seek benefit with an open mind and to take them up with sincere effort.
Whatever serves as a supportive condition for the Pure Land, one should practice it with diligence. Excellent, excellent! Rebirth according to one's wish through the primary and auxiliary practices.
Cultivating both [methods].
I exhort practitioners to cultivate from the fundamental source.
Whether they be great virtuous persons who are male or female, once they have already resolved their minds to practice, they must proceed from the fundamental source.

Cultivation and realization. What is meant by the "root"? It is to be loyal to the sovereign, filial to one's parents, respectful to teachers and elders, affectionate toward siblings, distinct in the roles of husband and wife, trustworthy toward friends, instructive toward children and grandchildren, harmonious with one's clan, reverent toward those of virtue, and forgiving toward the ignorant.
To persevere in these matters is what is called the work of entering the Path.
One will not be left in a state of aimless confusion. By practicing for a long time, one will eventually reach the level of the sages and worthies;

naturally, one will then enter the realm of the holy. Now, there may be those who practice, yet while they possess sincerity and reverence, they pay no attention whatsoever to the fundamental ground and do not investigate it at all.
I fear that the sages of the Three Teachings would certainly not accept such people, nor would they speak of loyalty and filial piety in their case.
These are people of benevolence and righteousness. Whether one holds office or not, the grace of the sovereign is beyond measure;
whether parents and teachers are living or deceased, they are all those to whom I owe profound gratitude. It is improper not to contemplate how to repay them.
Therefore, for those who resolve to practice the Way, regardless of whether their merit is great or small, and regardless of whether their recitations are many or few, [all are accounted].
All these are dedicated toward the Buddha, in order to repay the profound kindness of our sovereign, parents, teachers, and elders.

As for our other relatives—brothers, spouses, friends, children, grandchildren, and kinsmen—we should each consider how to transform them and instruct them so that they may achieve all wholesome fruits.
Only our parents give us life; if they had not given birth to us, from where would this body have come? Thus, their fundamental debt is most urgent, and we must strive to repay it.

This is especially urgent. It is by means of filial piety that the state governs the world; thus it is said that filial piety can be transferred into loyalty, and that loyal ministers are sought from the households of filial sons.
While one's parents are still living, what greater fortune could there be? You must exert all your strength to provide them with filial support.
One should gently and persistently exhort one's parents to serve the Buddha, causing them to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, so that they will surely attain Buddhahood in the future;

One must nevertheless diligently and earnestly practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name on their behalf and chant the scriptures.
One should earnestly entreat our Buddha through the Mahāyāna sūtras to receive one’s parents and lead them to rebirth in the Pure Land, doing so throughout one’s entire life;
only then can one be said to have fulfilled the way of a filial son. If one does not apply oneself to this, but practices solely for one's own sake, [one fails].
This refers to what is called "blind cultivation and reckless refinement. I fear that if the fundamental ground is deficient, it will be impossible to fulfill one's aspirations.
As the poem says: "The branches and leaves may not yet be harmed, but the roots are already pulled up.

If you apply yourself with a sincere heart to the fundamental ground, diligently practicing repentance—wherein "repentance" (chan) means repenting for past transgressions and "regret" (hui) means regretting present faults—then [success will follow].
Furthermore, it is said: "To err and not amend is what constitutes a true error. To err and yet be able to amend is a goodness greater than any other.

Furthermore, being able to resolve the mind to universally deliver all sentient beings so that they may together return to the Buddha-way and be liberated from the miserable realms of saṃsāra, this perfectly accords with the Buddha-mind.
Like a shadow following a form, one will certainly attain Buddhahood; as it is said, "By perfecting oneself, one can perfect others."
To benefit others is itself to benefit oneself.

This book is specially exhorted for those who uphold the Way to encourage all people in the world to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land to escape the suffering realms of saṃsāra.

May you enjoy eternal happiness. There may be those who have long venerated the Daoist teachings, or who gaze upon the stars and worship the Dipper, or who perform prostrations and recite the scriptures and repentances of the *Daozang*;

rather, because they have followed the Dao for many years, they are determined to cause them to abandon that path.
To abandon the mature and pursue the raw while single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name seems, at first glance, not an excellent method for exhorting others.

Furthermore...
