the Buddha ordained the cremation of deceased monks originally to enable them to leave behind their provisional, segmented forms and realize the true and eternal *dharmakāya*.
Consequently, since following the Buddha’s teaching, the monastic community has upheld this as a perpetual rule. However, as the path of the Dharma declined...
It is a long-standing degeneration. Nowadays, Buddhist disciples settle matters through cremation without adhering to established regulations;
often, they leave the remains in the shrine for only a single day before proceeding with cremation. Is this not a great violation of the Buddha’s precepts?

The Buddha taught that humans possess eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), which is to say, the faculty of cognition. The first five are called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses. The sixth...
Regarding consciousness, there is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the seventh manas-consciousness, and the eighth ālayavijñāna.
At the time of a person’s birth, it is this eighth consciousness that arrives first; the seventh, sixth, and fifth consciousnesses arrive in succession thereafter.
When they die, it is likewise this eighth consciousness that departs last; the other consciousnesses depart in succession beforehand. This is because...
The eighth consciousness is precisely the spiritual consciousness of a person; what the world calls the "soul" is this very thing.
Since this consciousness is spiritual, when a person first enters the mother's womb, it arrives beforehand; thus, while the child is in the mother’s belly, it is already an active entity.
After a person's life-force has been severed at death, this consciousness does not depart immediately, but must wait for...
The entire body becomes ice-cold, without a single trace of warmth; only then does that consciousness depart. Once the consciousness has departed, this body is entirely devoid of cognition.
If there is even one spot that remains slightly warm, the consciousness has not yet left, and it still perceives suffering.
At this time, one must strictly avoid putting on clothes; even shifting into a cross-legged posture or moving about is painful. It is simply that the mouth is unable to speak.
The body simply cannot move. The *Classic of Filial Piety* states that the three factors of life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are never separated from one another.
When a person possesses warmth, consciousness is present; as long as consciousness is present, the life-force has not yet been exhausted.

Therefore, throughout antiquity, there have been many instances where those who had died returned to life after three days. These accounts are recorded in the historical annals and can be verified in detail. Thus say the Confucians.

There is also the ritual of the great enshrouding on the third day. This is because of the affection and love felt toward one's kinsmen; they still hold out hope that there might be a chance of their being restored to life.
Now, we of the monastic community act in accordance with the natural order; although we do not harbor the deluded hope for their restoration to life, [we perform this rite].
How can you fail to empathize with their state of suffering and yet hastily set fire to them?
Where, then, is your compassionate heart? When a rabbit dies, even a fox grieves; each feels sorrow for its own kind.

If such is the case for mere creatures, how much more so for those who share the same human nature, and even more so for those of the same monastic class? When the extremity of human suffering is encountered, anger easily arises.
Because of a mind of anger, one immediately falls into ruin. As the sutra says: King Ajātaśatru established a Buddhist stupa and monastery; his merit was most magnificent.
At the moment of his death, an attendant holding a fan mistakenly let it fall onto the king's face. The king gave rise to a single thought of anger.
After death, one immediately falls into the body of a snake. Later, upon encountering a śramaṇa who preached the sūtras, they hear the Dharma and thereby attain rebirth in heaven.
Observing this, one can know that while the consciousness of the deceased has not yet departed, if the body is cremated, it will cause the being to give rise to anger due to the pain.
They fall even further, becoming the most wretched among the wretched. What enmity or resentment do I have toward the deceased that I would use my good intentions to perform such an evil deed?
If you say that these matters are vague and beyond verification, how can you not believe the Buddhist scriptures which record them in detail?
If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what other words can be trusted? Furthermore, why must one...
Are you not a disciple of the Buddha? Generally, those who give rise to [the funeral rites] do not pity the suffering of the deceased;
they merely seek to settle the matter quickly. Thus, they have no leisure to carefully examine the nuances of warmth and cold.

This has become their habitual practice, such that even when someone speaks of this principle, they instead laugh it off as pedantic. Consequently, the suffering of the deceased remains unexpressed. Alas, what an extreme state of affairs in this world!
As for suffering, it is nothing more than the loss of one's life. Life is like a live turtle escaping its shell; death is like a live crab falling into boiling water.
As the eight sufferings sear one from all sides, the pain is beyond description. In attending to the sick, one must simply exercise the utmost care and mindfulness.
Do not engage in idle chatter with the patient, which may cause them to form attachments. Likewise, avoid lamentation, clamor, and matters such as the funeral procession;
do not let the deceased know of these things. In general, exhort them to relinquish all worldly ties at once and focus the mind single-mindedly on the Buddha’s name.
If they do not prefer to recite the Buddha’s name, they should settle the mind in quiet contemplation to cultivate themselves.
Regarding the illness: follow the worldly customs. Wait until death has fully permeated the entire body; once the "master" has departed, wait another two or three hours before bathing and dressing.
If the body has become cold and stiff, wash it with hot water and apply a warm cloth to the deceased's arms and elbows;
the knees will soften of their own accord. When everything is prepared, simply request [the officiant].

Regarding people recollecting the Buddha, the *Zhengming lun* (Treatise on Clarifying the Sublime) states: For those who practice good, the warm breath moves from the bottom upward; for those who commit evil, it moves from the top downward.

When the entire body has cooled and the warm breath returns to the crown of the head, this is the path of the sages (*āryamārga*). If it reaches the eyes, one goes to the heavenly realm; if it reaches the heart, the human realm;
if it reaches the abdomen, the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*); if it reaches the knees, the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*); and if it reaches the soles of the feet, [one goes to the hells].
The path of hell. Yet, as for the great matter of birth and death, who among us can escape it?

No matter how much you may practice virtue throughout your life, if at the moment of death you give rise to a single evil thought, you will immediately fall into the evil realms. Conversely, if you have committed evil throughout your life but give rise to a single virtuous thought, you will be reborn in the good paths.
This is the final, decisive barrier; how can one not be cautious? How can one not be cautious?
